chunks: Why a ground plane shields signals. The question: Why can you use your ground plane to shield your signals?
A ground plane shields because it is a good conductor, and a good conductor does three things to nearby fields. It stops electric field lines, so they do not reach the other side.
It carries the return current, whose magnetic field cancels most of the trace's own.
And at higher frequencies, above a few MHz, currents induced in the copper soak up what is left.
A solid plane between two layers cuts the coupling between them a lot, as long as it has no slots or holes.
Picture a thick wall between two noisy rooms. A hole or gap in the wall lets sound leak straight through, and a thin wall does little against deep rumbles.
A ground plane is that wall. Slots and holes leak, and a thin copper plane does almost nothing against slow magnetic fields, such as 50 hertz hum from mains wiring.
Electric-field shielding in one picture. Without the plane, field lines from the aggressor terminate on the victim, which is capacitive coupling.
With a grounded plane between them, the lines terminate on the plane instead.
Electric field: the push a voltage exerts across space. Its field lines end on a conductor ("What capacitance is").
Return current: the equal and opposite current in the plane under a trace. Its field cancels the trace's field.
Mutual capacitance: the small capacitance between two traces that couples a signal from one to the other ("How signals couple and how to prevent it").
Aggressor and victim: the trace that makes the noise, and the trace that picks it up. Aperture: a slot or hole in the shield through which fields leak.
An aggressor trace swings 3. 3 volts and couples through 0. 5 picofarads to a victim input that has 5 picofarads to ground.
The capacitances split the voltage, so the victim sees 3. 3 times 0. 5 over (0. 5 plus 5) equals 0. 30 volts.
Put a grounded plane between them and the direct coupling falls to about 0. 05 picofarads (the page assumes a tenth). Now the victim sees 3. 3 times 0. 05 over (0.
05 plus 5) about 0. 033 volts, about nine times less. That is the whole idea.
"A ground plane is a good conductor, so it shields in three ways.
Electric field lines terminate on it instead of passing through, so a plane between two layers kills capacitive coupling.
The return current under the trace is equal and opposite to the signal current, so their magnetic fields cancel and the net field falls off fast.
And above a few MHz eddy currents absorb the field: about 47 decibels for 1 oz copper at 100 megahertz.
It only works if the plane is continuous, since slots and edges leak, and it does little against low-frequency magnetic fields."
